audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet Jehoahaz and Jehoash reigns, Elisha's final illness, arrow oracle, death, grave revival, and Aramean recovery narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for imperial oppression, military devastation, unnamed deliverer, Elisha's fatal illness, king's grief, embodied arrow ritual, prophetic anger over ambiguous performance, grave contact and revival, covenant compassion, and three military recoveries.

verses.restored: In twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years.
He did evil in eyes of YHWH and walked after sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin; he did not turn from them.
Anger of YHWH burned against Israel, and he gave them into hand of Hazael king of Aram and into hand of Ben-hadad son of Hazael all days.
Jehoahaz sought favor of YHWH, and YHWH listened to him, for he saw oppression of Israel, because king of Aram oppressed them.
YHWH gave Israel a deliverer, and they went out from under hand of Aram; children of Israel lived in their tents as before.
Nevertheless they did not turn from sins of house of Jeroboam, by which he caused Israel to sin, but walked in them; Asherah also remained standing in Samaria.
For he left to Jehoahaz from army only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because king of Aram had destroyed them and made them like dust for threshing.
Remaining acts of Jehoahaz, all he did, and his might, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Israel?
Jehoahaz lay with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. Joash his son became king in his place.
In thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel in Samaria, and reigned sixteen years.
He did evil in eyes of YHWH; he did not turn from all sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, but walked in them.
Remaining acts of Joash, all he did, and his might by which he fought Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Israel?
Joash lay with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat upon his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with kings of Israel.
Elisha became sick with sickness from which he died. Joash king of Israel came down to him, wept over his face, and said, My father, my father, chariot of Israel and its horsemen!
Elisha said to him, Take bow and arrows. He took bow and arrows.
He said to king of Israel, Put your hand upon bow. He put his hand, and Elisha placed his hands upon king's hands.
He said, Open window eastward. He opened it. Elisha said, Shoot. He shot. He said, Arrow of deliverance of YHWH, arrow of deliverance against Aram; you shall strike Aram at Aphek until finishing.
He said, Take arrows. He took them. He said to king of Israel, Strike ground. He struck three times and stopped.
Man of Divine became angry with him and said, You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck Aram until finishing it. Now three times you shall strike Aram.
Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of Moab entered land at coming of year.
As men were burying a man, look, they saw a band and threw man into grave of Elisha. When man touched bones of Elisha, he lived and stood upon his feet.
Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel all days of Jehoahaz.

YHWH was gracious to them, had compassion on them, and turned toward them because of covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; he was unwilling to destroy them or cast them from his presence until now.
Hazael king of Aram died, and Ben-hadad his son became king in his place.

Jehoash son of Jehoahaz returned and took from hand of Ben-hadad son of Hazael cities he had taken in war from hand of Jehoahaz his father. Three times Joash struck him and recovered cities of Israel.

translation_notes: Aramean oppression and destruction are described through royal theology, but civilians and ordinary soldiers bear the material devastation. No modern Syrian or Aramean community may be treated as an inherited enemy.
The unnamed 'deliverer' is not securely identified in the chapter. The ambiguity should remain rather than being forced into a preferred hero.
Elisha dies from illness. Prophetic stature does not guarantee cure, longevity, immunity, or spiritual failure-free health.
Joash's grief at Elisha's bedside is genuine within the narrative even though the king receives a negative royal evaluation.
The arrow ritual is symbolic and context-bound. It is not a divination or warfare technique for modern imitation.
Elisha becomes angry because Joash stops after three strikes, yet the instruction did not specify a number. This scene warns against leaders punishing others for unspoken expectations.
The promise to 'finish' Aram is violent war language and may not authorize extermination, genocide, or treating total destruction as faithful zeal.
The revival at Elisha's grave is an extraordinary narrative event, not a safe relic, corpse-contact, or resurrection procedure.
Touching bones does not establish that remains carry controllable spiritual power, and no bereaved family should be pressured to expect a miracle.
Covenant compassion interrupts destruction, while the military recovery remains partial and costly rather than a triumphal end to war.
safety_note: Do not stigmatize fatal illness, teach symbolic arrow or grave-contact techniques, punish people for failing hidden expectations, or turn Aram into a timeless enemy. Preserve Elisha's mortality, Joash's grief, the ambiguity of the deliverer, and the difference between covenant compassion and violent military victory.
